stress.name: stress
stress.description: Stress-monitoring profile for physiological time-series and task-induced variation.
stress.analysis_question: Does the monitored signal show a shift in regulatory range consistent with an allostatic stress response, or a failure to modulate that range?

signal_roles.primary_signal: Main physiological signal used to estimate stress-related dynamics.
signal_roles.condition: Task or context label used to compare stress and baseline states.
signal_roles.covariate: Optional metadata such as participant, session, or clinical notes.

interpretation_rules.sample_entropy: Allostatic accounts of stress treat a healthy system as one that can modulate its regulatory range on demand (Wiener, 1948); a rise in entropy from a tightly regulated baseline is consistent with a shift into a more reactive state, while a baseline that fails to show this contrast may indicate reduced regulatory flexibility rather than resilience.
interpretation_rules.spectral_entropy: Broader frequency dispersion under stress-related conditions is consistent with the recruitment of additional physiological subsystems (Ashby, 1956); a narrow, single-rhythm spectrum at baseline that persists under stress may indicate the system is not adaptively engaging alternate regulatory pathways.
interpretation_rules.dfa_exponent: Shifts in the DFA exponent away from a subject's own baseline reflect changes in how history-dependent the signal's fluctuations are (Bak, 1996; Jensen, 2007); treat this as a marker of altered regulatory dynamics under stress, not as a direct measure of how "complex" or "healthy" the system is.
interpretation_rules.mutual_information: Under an allostatic framing, physiological subsystems that recruit together under stress should show increased mutual information as they come under shared regulatory control (Wiener, 1948); persistently low coupling across conditions may indicate the signals are not part of the same stress-response pathway.

attention.name: attention
attention.description: Cognitive attention profile for task-driven dynamics and adaptive control.
attention.analysis_question: Does the monitored signal show tighter predictive precision when attention is engaged by the task, or reduced top-down control?

signal_roles.primary_signal: Main cognitive or neural signal associated with attentional state.
signal_roles.condition: Task phase, condition, or experimental state used for comparison.
signal_roles.covariate: Optional trial-level, session-level, or participant metadata.

interpretation_rules.sample_entropy: Attention can be framed as precision-weighting of expected sensory or task-relevant signals (Friston, 2010; Clark, 2013; Hohwy, 2013); reduced entropy when attention is engaged is consistent with tighter predictive precision around the task, while elevated entropy may reflect divided attention or reduced top-down control rather than richer processing.
interpretation_rules.spectral_entropy: A shift toward broader frequency engagement when attention is recruited is consistent with multiple task-relevant processes being active concurrently (Rumelhart et al., 1986); a narrower spectrum can indicate a single dominant rhythm capturing the bulk of signal energy.
interpretation_rules.dfa_exponent: Changes in long-range temporal correlation during attentional engagement point to shifts in how strongly past states constrain present ones (Hopfield, 1982); stronger persistence is consistent with sustained, attractor-like engagement, while a drop toward random-walk-like behavior (~0.5) suggests more moment-to-moment reactivity.
interpretation_rules.mutual_information: Under a predictive-processing account, attention coordinates precision-weighting across signals (Friston, 2010); increased mutual information when attention is engaged is consistent with shared top-down control linking the signals, while decreased coupling suggests they are being processed more independently.
